concepts.name: Establishment and Constitutional/Statutory Basis of NGT
key_dimensions: NGT Act 2010 as the parent statute vs. constitutional backing under Article 21 and 48A
India as only the third country after Australia and New Zealand to have a dedicated environmental tribunal
Mandate derived from Stockholm Conference 1972 and Rio Conference 1992 commitments
Distinction: NGT is a statutory body, NOT a constitutional body — a common UPSC trap

concepts.name: Composition and Qualifications of NGT Members
key_dimensions: Chairperson must be a retired Chief Justice of India or a Judge of the Supreme Court
Judicial members vs. Expert members — qualifications, eligibility, and minimum numbers (at least 10 each, up to 20 each)
Expert member qualifications: minimum 15 years of experience in environmental/forest/natural resource sector
Comparison trap: NGT Chairperson eligibility vs. NGT Judicial Member eligibility (Supreme Court judge vs. High Court judge)

concepts.name: Jurisdiction of NGT: Subject Matter and Territorial Scope
key_dimensions: Seven scheduled environmental laws over which NGT has jurisdiction (Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981, Environment Protection Act 1986, Forest Conservation Act 1980, Biological Diversity Act 2002, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991, National Environment Tribunal Act 1995)
Critical exclusion: Wildlife Protection Act 1972 and Indian Forest Act 1927 are NOT under NGT jurisdiction — high-yield trap
NGT's pan-India territorial jurisdiction with principal bench in Delhi and circuit benches
Distinction between NGT jurisdiction and High Court jurisdiction in environmental matters

concepts.name: NGT's Power to Award Compensation and Relief
key_dimensions: Principle of 'Polluter Pays' as the foundational basis for compensation awards
NGT can award compensation for damage to persons, property, and the environment simultaneously
No upper cap on compensation — contrast with many other quasi-judicial bodies that have monetary limits
Relief and compensation can be awarded even without proof of negligence (strict liability principle)

concepts.name: Limitation Period for Filing Applications Before NGT
key_dimensions: Standard limitation: 6 months from the date of cause of action
NGT has power to condone delay if sufficient cause is shown — conditional extension
Comparison trap: 6-month period for NGT vs. no statutory limitation for PIL in High Courts/Supreme Court
When does the cause of action 'arise' in environmental cases — continuous harm doctrine implications

concepts.name: Locus Standi Before the NGT
key_dimensions: Any person, including individuals, groups, and NGOs, can approach NGT — broad standing
No requirement to be personally aggrieved — contrast with traditional civil courts
Representative suits and public interest applications permissible before NGT
Comparison: NGT's liberal locus standi vs. strict locus standi in regular civil proceedings

concepts.name: Tenure, Service Conditions, and Removal of NGT Members
key_dimensions: Term: 5 years, not eligible for reappointment — ensures independence
Retirement age: 70 years for Chairperson, 67 years for other members
Removal process: Only by an order of the President on grounds of proven misbehavior or incapacity after Supreme Court inquiry
Comparison trap: Removal procedure of NGT members vs. removal of CAG, CEC — all involve inquiry but differ in procedural specifics

concepts.name: NGT's Appellate Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: NGT hears appeals against orders/decisions of regulatory authorities under the seven scheduled Acts
Time limit for filing appeal: 30 days from the date of communication of the order (extendable)
Who can appeal: Any aggrieved person including the government itself
Distinction: NGT as appellate body vs. NGT as original jurisdiction body — different procedural triggers

concepts.name: Powers of NGT: Civil Court Powers and Contempt
key_dimensions: NGT has powers of a civil court for purposes of taking evidence, enforcing attendance, and discovery of documents
NGT is NOT bound by the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 or the Indian Evidence Act — guided by principles of natural justice
NGT has power to punish for contempt of its own orders — akin to contempt powers of High Courts
Implication: NGT orders are as enforceable as a civil court decree — direct execution without referral to civil court

concepts.name: Appeals Against NGT Orders
key_dimensions: Appeals lie DIRECTLY to the Supreme Court of India — bypassing High Courts entirely
Time limit for appeal to Supreme Court: 90 days from the date of NGT award/order
High Court's jurisdiction is effectively ousted in matters within NGT's domain — landmark judicial clarification
Comparison trap: Unlike most tribunals where appeals go to High Court, NGT appeals go directly to Supreme Court

concepts.name: Precautionary Principle and Sustainable Development as Guiding Principles
key_dimensions: Section 20 of NGT Act mandates application of sustainable development, precautionary principle, and polluter pays principle
Precautionary principle: Burden of proof lies on the developer/polluter, not the victim
How NGT applies these principles in granting interim stays and injunctions
Judicial interpretation: NGT's use of precautionary principle vs. Supreme Court's interpretation in Vellore Citizens case

concepts.name: Interim Relief and Injunction Powers of NGT
key_dimensions: NGT can grant interim relief, including stay of project activities, pending final hearing
Balance of convenience and irreversibility of environmental damage as key criteria
Controversy: NGT's interim orders vs. government infrastructure projects — tension between development and environment
Comparison: NGT's power to stay environmental clearances vs. MoEF's power to grant/revoke them

concepts.name: Relationship Between NGT and High Courts: Jurisdictional Overlap and Conflict
key_dimensions: High Courts retain writ jurisdiction under Articles 226/227 even in environmental matters — NGT does not oust this
Supreme Court ruling: High Courts should generally not entertain PILs when NGT has jurisdiction (L. Chandra Kumar distinction)
Forum shopping issue: Parties approaching High Courts to bypass NGT — judicial trend to redirect to NGT
Situations where High Court jurisdiction is preferred over NGT — matters involving Wildlife Protection Act, constitutional questions

concepts.name: NGT's Role in Environmental Clearance (EC) Challenges
key_dimensions: NGT can examine grant or rejection of Environmental Clearances under EIA Notification 2006
Landmark cases: NGT quashing ECs for coal mines, infrastructure projects citing procedural lapses
Distinction: NGT reviews legality/procedure of EC, not merits of policy — boundary of judicial review
Interplay: MoEF & CC grants EC, NGT reviews it, Supreme Court may ultimately adjudicate — three-tier system

concepts.name: Circuit Benches and Zonal Structure of NGT
key_dimensions: Principal Bench: New Delhi; Four Circuit Benches: Bhopal (Central), Pune (Western), Kolkata (Eastern), Chennai (Southern)
Jurisdictional allocation of states among benches — UPSC may ask which bench covers which states
Practical importance: Accessibility to justice for environmental litigants across India
Challenges: Insufficient benches, pendency of cases, and calls for additional regional benches

concepts.name: Comparison of NGT with Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)
key_dimensions: NGT: Quasi-judicial body adjudicating disputes; CPCB: Regulatory/advisory body under Water Act 1974 and Air Act 1981
CPCB orders can be challenged before NGT — NGT has appellate authority over CPCB directions
Overlap in mandate: Both deal with pollution control but through fundamentally different mechanisms
UPSC trap: CPCB is statutory body under Water Act, NOT under Environment Protection Act — NGT is under NGT Act 2010

concepts.name: NGT and the Doctrine of Public Trust
key_dimensions: Public Trust Doctrine: State is a trustee of natural resources (air, water, forests) for public benefit
NGT has invoked Public Trust Doctrine to restrict commercial exploitation of natural commons
Origin: M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath case — Supreme Court first applied it; NGT subsequently expanded its use
Limitation: Doctrine applies only to public/state actors, not directly to private parties — NGT's workaround approaches

concepts.name: Criticism, Limitations, and Reform Proposals for NGT
key_dimensions: Shortage of expert members and vacancies — structural weakness undermining NGT's effectiveness
Lack of enforcement machinery: NGT relies on state governments and pollution control boards for compliance
Perceived judicial overreach: NGT sometimes accused of transgressing into policy domain (e.g., odd-even scheme, Aravallis)
Reform demands: Permanent benches in all states, independent enforcement wing, inclusion of Wildlife Act in Schedule

concepts.name: NGT vis-à-vis Environment Protection Act 1986 and MoEF
key_dimensions: EPA 1986 is one of the seven scheduled Acts — NGT can adjudicate violations under EPA
MoEF issues notifications under EPA (e.g., EIA 2006, CRZ Notification) which are subject to NGT scrutiny
Distinction: MoEF makes environmental policy; NGT adjudicates disputes arising from that policy — separation of functions
Critical case: NGT striking down parts of EIA Draft 2020 notification — limits of executive environmental policymaking

concepts.name: Financial Penalties, Restoration Costs, and Disbursement Mechanism
key_dimensions: NGT can direct payment of compensation into an 'Environmental Relief Fund' for future claimants
Restoration of environment to its original state can be ordered at the cost of the polluter
Joint and several liability: All contributors to environmental damage can be held jointly liable
Comparison trap: Environmental Relief Fund under NGT Act vs. Environment Protection Fund under EPA 1986 — different instruments
